div.head: ECf 32 C 2
div.ab: Ita constituit optimus Yne rex Anglorum, qui electus fuit in regem per Angliam et qui primo optinuit monarchiam tocius regni huius post aduentum Anglorum in Britanniam. Fuit enim primus rex coronatus Anglorum et Britonum simul manentium in Britannia post aduentum Saxonum Germanie in Britannia, scilicet post acceptam fidem a beato Gregorio per sanctum Augustinum.
div.note: Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 658 (November 2026): read from the page images and checked against the scan’s own text layer, differences settled against the page.

This passage is not part of ECf or ECf retr: it is one of the additions of the London collection (Leges Anglorum s. XIII in. Londoniis collectae), which Liebermann prints across the page as an insertion into ECf retr. 32 (32 A–E, pp. 655–660). The dictionary cites it as “ECf 32 C …”, so it is kept with ECf here.
Liebermann marks “aduentum” and “acceptam” with daggers for his marginal dates, 449 and 596.

note.seg: der Londoner schiebt Ine auch sonst Recht und Politik vom Ende des 12. Jhs. unter; zwar steht dieser Abschnitt in den Concilia M. Brit. Spelman’s 219 und Wilkins’ I 74, gilt aber als Fabel schon Spelman, Henschen Acta sanct., Febr. 6, und Mabillon Acta sanct. Bened. III 494

the Londoner elsewhere too foists law and policy of the late 12th century on Ine; this section does stand in Spelman’s Concilia M. Brit. 219 and Wilkins’ I 74, but already Spelman, Henschen (Acta sanct., Feb. 6) and Mabillon (Acta sanct. Bened. III 494) regard it as a fable
the monarch is to appear an elected king
so lügt der Londoner schon vorher: meine Leg. Angl. S. 14. Auch Ralf Niger macht Ine von Wessex (s. o. S. 88) zum ersten König ganz Englands
the Londoner lies thus already earlier: my Leg. Angl. p. 14. Ralph Niger too makes Ine of Wessex (see above, p. 88) the first king of all England
Pr. e. fu. Co Or Ld
Pr. e. fu. Co Or Ld

div.ab: So decreed the most excellent Ine, king of the English, who was elected king throughout England and who first obtained the monarchy of this whole kingdom after the coming of the English into Britain. For he was the first crowned king of the English and of the Britons dwelling together in Britain after the coming of the Saxons of Germany into Britain, namely after the faith was received from blessed Gregory through Saint Augustine.
